notes: Every entry is grounded in a real, verifiable source. No statistic, author, or DOI in this file is fabricated. Where studies disagree or where evidence is contested, that disagreement is preserved in 'evidence_notes' instead of being smoothed over. 'evidence_type' distinguishes systematic/meta-analytic evidence from single regional studies from qualitative scientific consensus, and 'confidence' reflects how strongly the retrieved evidence supports the stated effect for a NEW, unmeasured site.

documents.title: Optimizing cover cropping application for sustainable crop production
documents.authors: He, Q., Lu, C., Cowie, A., Zhao, S., Liu, D.L., Yi, B., Shi, L., Zhang, S., Qiu, T., Shi, Y., Huete, A., Siddique, K.H.M., Yu, Q., Li, L.
documents.mechanism: Cover crops add year-round living root biomass and residue, feeding soil microbial communities that build organic carbon; legumes additionally fix atmospheric nitrogen, which further stimulates microbial carbon processing.
documents.finding_summary: Across a global synthesis, legume cover crops increased soil organic carbon (SOC) by 5.9% and crop yield by 16.0% relative to no cover crop; non-legume cover crops increased SOC by 4.0%. The SOC/yield gains came with a trade-off of 36.2% higher nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions, an important climate caveat.
documents.evidence_notes: This is the strongest single source in the KB for a general SOC effect size because it pools thousands of field observations. Smaller regional studies below report larger effects (up to +23-38%), showing real site-to-site variability; the 5-9% figure is the safer global central estimate.

documents.title: Global meta-analysis of cover crop effects on soil organic carbon fractions
documents.source: Peer-reviewed manuscript, global synthesis of 93 studies
documents.mechanism: Cover crop residue and root exudates increase labile carbon fractions (microbial biomass carbon, dissolved and particulate organic carbon) before that carbon stabilizes into longer-term mineral-associated organic carbon, improving soil aggregation and microbial habitat.
documents.finding_summary: Compared to bare soil, cover crops increased total SOC by 12% and increased seven measured SOC fractions, including microbial biomass carbon by 33% and particulate organic carbon by 15%. Effects were strongest in Entisols and Ultisols and grew with experimental duration.

quantitative_effect.magnitude: +12% total SOC vs bare soil; microbial biomass carbon +33%

documents.evidence_notes: Compares cover crop vs bare fallow (not vs a growing cash crop), so this is an upper-bound style comparison; effect grows with time under cover crop.

documents.title: Legume cover crops enhance soil organic carbon via microbial necromass in orchard alleyways
documents.authors: Hu, Q., Jiang, T., Thomas, B.W., Chen, J., Xie, J., Hu, Y., Kong, F., Yang, Y., Chen, X., Zhang, Y., Shi, X.
documents.evidence_type: multi-site regional field study (7 orchards, China)
documents.mechanism: Legume cover crops raise dissolved organic carbon and nitrogen availability, which drives greater microbial biomass and turnover; microbial necromass (dead microbial biomass) becomes a major building block of stable soil carbon.
documents.finding_summary: Legume cover crops increased SOC by 23% versus bare-soil control plots, compared to only 2% for non-legume cover crops in the same orchards, driven largely by bacterial and fungal necromass carbon accumulation.
documents.evidence_notes: Effect size is much larger than the global meta-analysis (kb001) — a reminder that local soil type, climate, and cropping system strongly moderate outcomes; treat the 23% figure as a plausible upper range for favorable conditions, not a universal constant.

documents.title: Agroforestry: an elixir for soil health management and carbon sequestration
documents.authors: Sivakumar, K., Manimaran, G., Tilak, M., Ramah, K., Sivasakthivelan, P., Rogan, H.B., Vishal, R.
documents.mechanism: Deep-rooted trees add below-ground biomass carbon and litter beyond what annual crops reach, improve nutrient cycling and water retention, and add structural/habitat diversity that annual monocultures lack.
documents.finding_summary: Reviewed estimates show agroforestry systems can sequester roughly 0.29 to 15.2 Mg C per hectare per year depending on system type (alley cropping, silvopasture, etc.), soil, and climate, alongside improved nitrogen use efficiency and reduced erosion.

quantitative_effect.magnitude: 0.29-15.2 Mg C ha-1 yr-1 (wide range, system-dependent)

documents.evidence_notes: Wide range reflects genuinely high variability across system designs; report as a range, not a point estimate, when advising a specific farm.

documents.title: Agroforestry system improves soil carbon and nitrogen stocks after land-use change in the Brazilian semi-arid region
documents.authors: Tonucci, R.G., Vogado, R.F., Silva, R.D., Pompeu, R.C.F.F., Oda-Souza, M., Souza, H.A. de
documents.source: Revista Brasileira de Ciência do Solo, 47, e0220124
documents.evidence_type: regional field study (semi-arid Brazil, Caatinga biome)
documents.mechanism: Retaining native woody rows within a cropped semi-arid field maintains deeper root systems and litter input through the dry season, sustaining soil carbon and nitrogen stocks that a cleared monoculture loses.
documents.finding_summary: Agroforestry systems that retained native woody forest rows (33-66% of the plot) showed improved soil carbon and nitrogen stocks at depth compared to cleared intercropping-only plots in a semi-arid region, directly relevant to low-rainfall monoculture settings.

quantitative_effect.magnitude: improved vs monoculture intercropping (study reports stocks, not a single %)

documents.evidence_notes: Directly relevant to semi-arid, low-organic-carbon, monoculture scenarios similar to the hackathon's example use case.

documents.title: Is habitat fragmentation bad for biodiversity? (and the Fletcher et al. 2018 rebuttal)
documents.authors: Fahrig, L. (2017 review); Fletcher, R.J. et al. (2018 rebuttal)
documents.evidence_type: systematic review + contested rebuttal (contradictory evidence, preserved intentionally)
documents.mechanism: Habitat AMOUNT loss removes resources and population capacity directly. Habitat FRAGMENTATION per se (splitting the same total habitat area into more, smaller patches) is a separate, more debated effect on edge exposure, connectivity, and generalist vs. specialist species response.
documents.finding_summary: Habitat loss is uncontested as harmful to biodiversity. But fragmentation independent of habitat amount is genuinely disputed in the literature: Fahrig's review found most landscape-scale responses were non-significant, and of significant ones, most were positive; Fletcher et al. (2018) directly dispute this reading of the evidence and argue fragmentation per se is generally harmful.

quantitative_effect.magnitude: not a single number - active scientific disagreement

documents.evidence_notes: Deliberately kept as contested evidence. The system should never claim 'fragmentation always reduces species richness by X%' - that would be a fabricated certainty the literature does not support. It should instead say habitat AMOUNT is the safer, well-supported lever.

documents.title: Riparian Buffer Width, Vegetative Cover, and Nitrogen Removal Effectiveness (literature synthesis)
documents.authors: North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality, drawing on Osborne & Kovacic (1993) and Neuse basin field research
documents.source: NC DEQ riparian buffer science review
documents.evidence_type: government literature synthesis of peer-reviewed field studies
documents.region: southeastern USA (Neuse River basin) + broader literature
documents.mechanism: Vegetated buffer strips along waterways slow surface runoff, let sediment settle, and support root-zone microbial denitrification that converts excess nitrate to inert N2 gas before it reaches the stream; buffer vegetation also adds wildlife habitat and shades water to moderate temperature.
documents.finding_summary: Buffers of 100-165 ft width reduced total nitrogen loading to streams by up to 85% or more; narrower buffers were markedly less effective (49 ft buffers reduced nitrogen by 48%, 26 ft buffers by only 28% in Neuse basin research), showing effectiveness scales strongly with width.
documents.evidence_notes: Width-response relationship is unusually well quantified for a water-quality intervention; use with land-use and biodiversity variables together since it also restores habitat corridors.

documents.title: Drylands and Land Degradation (issues brief, drawing on IPCC/UNCCD assessments)
documents.authors: IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature)
documents.mechanism: Deforestation, overgrazing, and unsustainable cultivation strip dryland vegetation cover; without cover, soil erodes and loses nutrients and moisture-holding capacity, which directly kills the soil bacteria, fungi, and insects that underpin dryland food webs - a mutually reinforcing (cause AND outcome) decline loop.
documents.finding_summary: An estimated 25-35% of the world's drylands are already degraded (desertified), affecting over 250 million people directly; soil biodiversity loss is simultaneously a cause and a consequence of that degradation.
documents.evidence_notes: Global figure, not farm-specific - use as context for regional risk, not as a site-level prediction.

documents.title: IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land (SRCCL)
documents.mechanism: Degraded land has reduced vegetation and organic matter, lowering its capacity to absorb and store carbon; this weakens a natural climate buffer, which in turn worsens the heat and drought stress that further degrades land - a reinforcing feedback loop between land condition and climate.
documents.finding_summary: The IPCC concludes land degradation reduces productivity and the soil's ability to absorb carbon, which exacerbates climate change, while climate change in turn worsens land degradation; some degradation can become irreversible if action is delayed, making early, sustainable land management important.

quantitative_effect.magnitude: qualitative - no single global percentage given

documents.evidence_notes: High-level assessment consensus; use for framing urgency and feedback loops, not for site-specific numeric estimates.
documents.confidence: high (for the qualitative mechanism), not applicable (no numeric estimate)

documents.title: Conservation agriculture and reduced tillage - established soil science consensus
documents.authors: FAO Conservation Agriculture programme (general scientific consensus, multiple primary studies)
documents.mechanism: Minimizing soil disturbance preserves fungal hyphal networks and soil aggregate structure, which protects organic carbon from rapid oxidation, improves water infiltration and moisture retention, and preserves habitat for soil macrofauna (earthworms, ground beetles) that till and fertilize soil biologically.
documents.finding_summary: Reduced/no-till combined with permanent soil cover and crop rotation (FAO's three conservation agriculture principles) is well established to improve soil structure, water infiltration, and soil biodiversity relative to intensive tillage, though the magnitude is highly soil- and climate-dependent and not reduced to one universal number.

quantitative_effect.magnitude: directionally positive; magnitude is site-dependent, not quantified here

documents.evidence_notes: Intentionally left unquantified rather than inventing a percentage - this is a case where the system should say 'evidence supports the direction, not a specific number' per the project's anti-fabrication rule.
documents.confidence: medium (qualitative direction well-supported; no safe universal magnitude)

documents.title: Crop diversification, polyculture and pollinator/pest-regulation services - established agroecology consensus
documents.authors: General agroecology literature synthesis (FAO agrobiodiversity programme)
documents.mechanism: Monocultures offer a single resource pulse in time and space, favoring a narrow set of pest and generalist species; interplanting multiple crop species and flowering strips provides staggered floral resources and habitat structure that supports a wider range of pollinators and natural pest predators, which in turn reduces monoculture-associated pest outbreaks.
documents.finding_summary: Diversifying monocultures via intercropping, crop rotation, or flowering strips is well-established in agroecology to increase functional biodiversity (pollinators, natural enemies of pests) relative to single-crop systems, though effect sizes vary widely by crop, region, and landscape context.

quantitative_effect.magnitude: directionally positive; magnitude not quantified here (highly context-dependent)

documents.evidence_notes: Paired with kb001/kb002/kb003 (cover crops) and kb004/kb005 (agroforestry) for monoculture wheat / semi-arid scenarios like the hackathon's example use case.

documents.title: Soil pH and nutrient/microbial availability - established soil chemistry consensus
documents.authors: General soil science consensus (FAO Global Soil Partnership)
documents.mechanism: Most agricultural plants and soil microbes function best in a moderately acidic-to-neutral pH range (roughly 6.0-7.5); outside that range, key nutrients (phosphorus, and micronutrients at high pH; aluminum toxicity risk at low pH) become less available or toxic, suppressing both plant growth and microbial/faunal activity that drives organic matter cycling.
documents.finding_summary: Extreme soil pH (strongly acidic or alkaline) is well established to suppress nutrient availability and microbial activity, indirectly constraining the soil organic carbon buildup and plant productivity that underpin aboveground biodiversity.

quantitative_effect.magnitude: qualitative - depends on specific pH deviation and crop

documents.evidence_notes: Used to flag when a reported soil pH value is a likely constraint worth raising even if no other variable was mentioned.
